## Problem

Let \(B(0,1)\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be the unit ball. Determine for which \(s\in\mathbb{R}\),

\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{|x|^s}\,dx < +\infty.
\]

## Solution

The only possible singularity of the integrand is at the origin. Using polar coordinates,

\[
x=r\omega,\qquad r\in(0,1),\quad \omega\in S^{n-1},
\]

and

\[
dx=r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\omega.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{|x|^s}\,dx
=
\int_{S^{n-1}}\int_0^1 r^{-s}r^{n-1}\,dr\,d\omega
=
|S^{n-1}|\int_0^1 r^{n-1-s}\,dr.
\]

Recall that

\[
\int_0^1 r^\alpha\,dr<+\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha>-1.
\]

Hence the integral is finite if and only if

\[
n-1-s>-1,
\]

that is,

\[
\boxed{s<n}.
\]

More precisely, when \(s<n\),

\[
\int_{B(0,1)} \frac{1}{|x|^s}\,dx
=
\frac{|S^{n-1}|}{n-s}.
\]

When \(s=n\), the radial integral becomes

\[
\int_0^1 \frac{dr}{r},
\]

which diverges logarithmically; when \(s>n\), it diverges even more strongly.

## Remark

This is a basic example of the general principle that, in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), a point singularity of order \(|x|^{-s}\) is locally integrable near the origin exactly when \(s<n\).
